bio.text: Lkhagvasuren Ganbold is the Founder and Executive Director of Tsets Partners Law Firm. He is an attorney at law with 12 years of experience specializing in insurance law and business law.

He holds a Master of Laws (LL.M.) from Ikh Zasag Law School and a Master of Business Administration (MBA) from the University of Finance and Economics (UFE). He is currently a Ph.D. candidate at the School of Law, National University of Mongolia. He is a member of the Mongolian Bar Association and the Association of Mongolian Advocates.

Since 2025, he has been serving as an arbitrator at the Mongolian International Arbitration Center, and in 2026, he was appointed as an arbitrator at the Mongolian International and National Sports Arbitration.

Bat-Erdene Bayarsaikhan is a Co-Founder of Tsets Partners Law Firm. He is an attorney at law with 12 years of experience specializing in criminal law, business law, and corporate law. He holds a Bachelor's and Master's degree in Law from Ikh Zasag Law School. He is a member of the Mongolian Bar Association and the Association of Mongolian Advocates.

Tsagandorjiin Erdenebold graduated from Kyiv State University of the Russian Federation (the Soviet Union at that time) as an International Lawyer, and from the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom as an English Translator. He also holds doctorate degrees from the Institute of State and Law of the Russian Federation and The George Washington University in the United States.
Work Experience
He has rich experience working in legal counsel and management positions across the public sector, private sector, and international organizations.

Government Sector: Served as a Referent at the Executive Office of the Presidium of the People's Great Hural, Foreign Policy Advisor to the State Great Hural (Parliament) of Mongolia, Head of the Foreign Relations Department of the Governor's Office of the Capital City, and Advisor to the Minister of Mining and Heavy Industry. He has also managed projects related to international trade, GATT, and UNCITRAL for the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and continues to serve as a contracted translator for UNDP to this day.

Private Sector: Worked as a representative of the U.S. law firm "Buxbaum & Choy," pioneering international consulting services in Mongolia. Subsequently, he co-founded the international law firm "New Grata JLPV" with foreign lawyers and served as its Executive Director. His experience includes assisting "Energy Resources" company with its listing on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, helping Mongolian companies trade shares on the U.S. NASDAQ exchange, and serving as an international legal advisor for the Power Plant project of "Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi" company. Most recently, he worked as the Head of the Legal Department at "New Ulaanbaatar International Airport" LLC.

University & Research: Contributed to training future lawyers by serving as Director of the School of Humanities at the Mongolian University of Science and Technology, Visiting Professor at Mahidol University in Thailand, and Professor at the National University of Mongolia and CITY University. During this time, he has published over 20 books, textbooks, and research articles.
Awards
Awarded Mongolia's State Supreme Honor, the "Order of the Polar Star" (Altan Gadas), and the title of "Leading Worker in Education."
Languages
Fully proficient in Mongolian, Russian, and English, with knowledge of French.

article.sourceLabel: View the original post on Facebook

body: Article 10.3 of the Regulation on Commissioning Buildings and Structures, revised by Government Resolution No. 212 of 2021, prohibited a commissioning commission from working on a building found to have been used unless the matter had first been resolved by a court.

Attorney B. Bat-Erdene of Tsets Partners challenged whether this restriction complied with the law. After the case was heard at all three court levels, the Supreme Court of Mongolia upheld the complaint and invalidated Article 10.3.

While the provision remained in force, authorities treated the placement of equipment, furniture, or other items in a building as evidence that the building had been used and, on that basis, declined to convene a commissioning commission.
The Construction Law, however, contains no rule permitting an application for a commissioning commission to be rejected, or the commission itself to be prohibited, on that ground.
Invalidating Article 10.3 therefore has an important legal effect on the building commissioning process.
Where an applicant satisfies the statutory requirements and applies to commission a building, the competent authority may no longer refuse to convene the commission on a ground not provided by law.

The placement of equipment or furniture alone cannot be treated as conclusive proof of use. A commission must proceed under the applicable law and regulations and decide whether the building may be commissioned based on the actual circumstances and statutory requirements.
keyPoints: Protects the rights of applicants seeking to commission a building.
Limits administrative refusals based on grounds not provided by law.
Brings the commissioning process into line with statutory requirements.
Protects the lawful rights and interests of individuals and legal entities.

body: This article provides a practical overview of the main legal rules and considerations relevant to the topic.
In addition to statutory requirements, the organization should review whether its internal policies, agreements, and decision-making procedures operate consistently with one another.

Looking at a single agreement or document in isolation is rarely enough to identify the full legal risk. The rights and duties of each party, information-sharing procedures, and liability provisions should be considered together.

Unclear authority, approval levels, or document-execution procedures can increase the likelihood of disputes during implementation. Mapping internal approvals, signatures, and record keeping in advance helps create a reliable process.

Before implementing a change, existing documents should be reviewed and any conflicting or duplicated provisions aligned. The people and counterparties affected by the change should also receive clear and timely information.

Decisions, approvals, and material communications should be retained in a form that can be verified later. For a specific matter, professional legal advice can help define the risks and the steps that should be taken in advance.
keyPoints: Check that the relevant agreements, policies, and decisions are consistent with one another.
State each party's rights, duties, timelines, payment terms, and liability clearly.
Keep changes, approvals, and material communications in a verifiable form.

body: In this Business MN episode, Tsets Partners founder and attorney G. Lkhagvasuren discusses disputes commonly encountered in business and practical ways to protect legal interests before problems arise.

The conversation emphasizes reviewing the substance of a document, the parties' rights and duties, and liability terms before an executive signs it. It also explains why a generic contract downloaded from the internet may not reflect a business's actual circumstances or risks.

Recording agreements, responsibilities, and material communications in writing—and preserving supporting evidence—creates an essential foundation for protecting a party's position if a dispute occurs.
The episode also covers disputes with foreign partners, legal risk protection when starting a business, founder disputes, and the importance of a properly tailored company charter.
keyPoints: Review the rights, duties, liabilities, and risks in full before signing an agreement.
Confirm oral agreements and material communications in writing and retain the supporting record.
Do not rely on a generic template; tailor contracts and the company charter to the actual business.

body: In this episode of Terminal 1.0's Law and Legal Affairs program, Tsets Partners managing director and attorney G. Lkhagvasuren discusses how businesses can align their operations with the law.
Organizing business decisions, day-to-day operations, and documentation in line with applicable legislation is a foundation for managing legal risk before it becomes a dispute.
Legal requirements are most effective when considered during planning and decision-making, rather than only after a problem has already arisen.
Because every organization has a different structure and operating context, compliance should be assessed against its actual circumstances and professional legal advice obtained where appropriate.
keyPoints: Align business operations, decisions, and documentation with applicable legislation.
Manage legal risk through planning and internal processes before an issue arises.
Assess compliance against the organization's actual circumstances and seek professional advice where needed.

interview.intro: An interview with G. Lkhagvasuren, Founding Partner and Attorney at Tsets Partners, a professional law firm providing legal advisory services for the day-to-day operations of businesses.

sections.title: Tsets Partners and Its Practice
paragraphs: Established in 2017, Tsets Partners Law Firm currently operates two offices in Ulaanbaatar and employs four attorneys and six legal assistants. Over the past eight years, the number of organizations maintaining long-term cooperation with the firm has continued to grow.

Regular clients include Alco Group, Practical Insurance, Milaya Foods, and the Agricultural Corporation SOE LLC. The firm provides ongoing legal advice, debt recovery support, contract drafting and negotiation, assistance in tender procedures, dispute resolution, and other legal support across business activities.
sections.quote: In the day-to-day operations of businesses, numerous legal risks arise, particularly when entering into major contractual arrangements. Our priority is to anticipate such uncertainties and ensure that contracts clearly stipulate solutions to potential disputes.

sections.title: Education and Professional Experience
paragraphs: G. Lkhagvasuren obtained a Master’s degree in Business Administration from the University of Finance and Economics between 2020 and 2022. He continues to manage Tsets Partners LLC while pursuing doctoral studies in law at the National University of Mongolia.
He specializes in insurance law and previously served as Head of the Claims Department at Practical Insurance for four years, gaining extensive professional experience in the insurance sector.

Entrepreneurs who address legal uncertainty at the earliest stage and seek professional advice can protect themselves from many potential risks. Legal services are comparable to chess: they are a strategic tool that enables you to foresee risks three moves ahead.

sections.title: Research on Court Decisions in Insurance Disputes
paragraphs: G. Lkhagvasuren published a research paper titled “Analysis of Court Decisions in Insurance Disputes” on the Legal Data platform. It examines how Mongolian courts resolved insurance-related disputes between 2019 and 2024.

A similar study was conducted in Mongolia in 2016. By 2024, however, both the business environment and insurance contracts had changed significantly, making it necessary to examine how courts currently resolve such disputes.

Since 2019, he has taught Insurance Law and the Application of Law to senior law students at Ikh Zasag International University. He selected three students as assistant researchers for the project. The report gives citizens a general understanding of insurance issues and provides legal practitioners with practical guidance on judicial interpretation and application.

The study found that most insurance disputes arise when policyholders cannot obtain compensation. In more than 70 percent of the disputes studied, courts ruled in favor of compensation. The findings indicate that insurers sometimes refuse claims without sufficient legal grounds, while many people do not pursue litigation because they perceive it as burdensome.

sections.title: International Cooperation
paragraphs: In 2025, the firm planned to enter into cooperation agreements with law firms in the People’s Republic of China. Many Mongolian companies receive investment, equipment, and materials from China, and the two countries maintain extensive cooperation across multiple sectors. Because many of the firm’s clients are Chinese citizens and legal entities, cooperation with Chinese law firms has become a practical necessity.
The firm is also working to increase the number of Chinese-speaking lawyers so that legal teams from both jurisdictions can cooperate effectively when cross-border disputes or other matters arise.

sections.title: Professional Values
paragraphs: G. Lkhagvasuren believes that law firms should not rely heavily on self-promotional marketing and that word-of-mouth is the most effective form of reputation. Clients should feel that every possible effort has been made on their behalf. Genuine, continuous relationships in which clients feel they have a personal attorney are the strongest form of professional trust.

Legal practice can also involve psychological reassurance. People often seek help while facing serious debt or unjust liability. Once they understand their legal protections, rights, and obligations, they can leave with renewed confidence and hope. Providing that support alongside legal advice is one reason he takes pride in the profession.
sections.quote: Attorneys not only protect people from losses caused by a lack of legal knowledge; they also help create economic stability and peace of mind by safeguarding their legal rights and interests.
